nameStory: Black-eye Lichen gets its striking name from its dark, round reproductive structures called apothecia that look like tiny black eyes peering out from the lichen's surface. These 'eyes' create such a distinctive pattern that early naturalists couldn't help but see the resemblance to a watchful gaze from the rock face.
description: Black-eye Lichen is a crustose lichen that forms thin, crusty patches directly on rock surfaces, looking almost like gray paint that's been splattered and dried. The most eye-catching feature is its collection of small, jet-black, round discs (apothecia) that dot the surface like tiny buttons or eyes. This lichen typically forms patches a few inches across, though older specimens can spread to cover areas the size of a dinner plate or larger.

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Look for the signature small, perfectly round, jet-black discs scattered across the surface - these 'black eyes' are unmistakable and feel smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms a thin, crusty coating that's firmly attached to rock - you can't peel it off like you might with leafy lichens

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: The main body appears pale gray to whitish, creating a strong contrast with the dark reproductive discs

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost always found growing directly on hard rock surfaces, especially granite and other acidic stones

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: The surface feels rough and gritty, like fine sandpaper, with the black discs standing out as smooth spots

habitat: Black-eye Lichen favors exposed rock faces and boulders, particularly granite outcrops and stone walls throughout New England's mountains and hills. You'll often spot it on sunny, well-ventilated rock surfaces where it can get plenty of light and air circulation. It seems to prefer acidic rock types and can be found from sea level up into the mountains.

seasonality.spring: The contrast between the gray body and black 'eyes' becomes more pronounced as spring rains moisten the lichen, making it easier to spot against wet rock faces.
seasonality.summer: During dry summer weather, the lichen may appear more faded and chalky, but the distinctive black reproductive discs remain clearly visible and are at their most active.
seasonality.fall: Fall moisture brings out the lichen's colors again, and this is often when new black reproductive discs become most noticeable as they mature.
seasonality.winter: Even under snow, this hardy lichen persists on exposed rock faces, and winter's bare landscape often makes rock-dwelling lichens more visible and accessible for observation.

funFact: Black-eye Lichen has managed to colonize rocks on every continent, including Antarctica, making it one of the most successful world travelers in the lichen kingdom - all without ever leaving its rock home!
confusionNotes: The distinctive black 'eyes' make this lichen quite unique, but beginners might confuse it with other gray crustose lichens before the reproductive discs develop. Remember: if you see those perfect little black circles on gray crust, you've found your Black-eye Lichen.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its dramatic common name, Black-eye Lichen is actually quite rare in New England, with only a few confirmed sightings, so finding one would be a special discovery worth reporting to local naturalist groups.
compareHints: Black-eye Lichen is the only member of its genus Tephromela found in New England, making it unique in the region. It differs from other gray crustose lichens in the same family by its distinctive perfectly round, jet-black apothecia that create such a striking 'polka-dot' pattern. While other rock lichens might have dark reproductive structures, none have quite the same bold, eye-like appearance.
